title: Willow garden trug
subtitle: A flat-based harvesting basket for cut flowers and vegetables
excerpt: A willow garden trug: an oval, flat-based, open-sided basket 45 cm long, 25 cm wide, 15 cm deep. Brown willow stakes, buff weavers, a fixed D-shaped handle at each end. The open weave drains water and lets air circulate, which suits it for harvesting, carrying tools, or bringing in cut herbs.

glossaryTerms.definition: The upright structural rods of a basket that form the frame for the woven sides. Stakes are heavier-gauge rods than weavers.
The thinner rods woven between the stakes to build up the sides of the basket.
A pointed steel spike used to open up the weave to insert new rods or to thread the border work.

content.text: A garden trug differs from a shopping basket in its low depth (15 cm versus 20 cm) and its D-shaped carrying handles rather than looped ones. The trug sits on the ground between the gardener's feet and is lifted by one or both handles; the low depth makes it easy to reach in and remove harvested produce without tipping. The flat base sets this apart from a round-base basket: all the cross-weave on the base is at the same level, which gives the trug a stable base on uneven ground.
Base sticks: 8 brown willow rods, 35 to 55 cm alternating, 8 mm at butt. Stakes: 26 brown willow rods, 75 cm, 7 mm at butt.
: 80 buff willow rods, 1 to 1.2 m. Handle rods: 2 thick brown willow rods, 80 cm, 12 mm at butt (these form the D-shaped arched handles).

Build a flat-frame oval base: two long rods laid parallel 20 cm apart, with six shorter cross-sticks lashed between them using pairing weave. The lashed base is the full 45 cm length. Unlike the round slath base, the trug base cross-sticks radiate across the frame at equal spacings rather than from a central point.

, form the two D-shaped handle arches. Soak the two handle rods until fully pliable. Bend each into a D shape 20 cm across and 15 cm tall, and push both ends of the arch down into the base beside the outermost base sticks at each short end. The arch stands free while the staking proceeds; it will be locked in during the upsetting wale.

. Fold stakes upright. Weave three rounds of four-rod wale for the upset, weaving over the base of each handle arch to lock it in. Use the rapping iron to press each wale round down firmly.

Side with buff pairing weave in the same manner as the round basket, to 12 cm height. On the trug, the siding keeps a slight outward flare. The sides of a trug are noticeably lower than a shopping basket; this flare is what gives it stability.

Three rounds of four-rod wale at the rim. Work a straightforward three-rod behind-one border. The border meets the base of each handle arch at the short ends: tuck these border ends behind the arch rod rather than into the weave.

attrs.symptom: The handle arch bent to one side during upsetting
attrs.cause: The wale weave was tighter on one side than the other as it passed over the arch base.
attrs.fix: If the arch is still flexible, re-centre it by hand and clamp with a clothes peg until the wale is complete. Once the wale dries, the arch will be held by the weave.

attrs.symptom: The base is not flat, it has a slight dome
attrs.cause: Pairing tension pulled the frame into a curve.
attrs.fix: Weight the base with a flat board while the pairing is still wet. A domed base on a garden trug wobbles on uneven ground.
